description: Solo team from São Paulo, Brazil. I build web tools on top of open data, working with AI coding assistants. This weekend I'm taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: using NASA lunar topography to show when the Sun and Earth are visible from landing sites near the Moon's south pole, and what that means for a mission. Not recruiting this year, but always happy to trade ideas with other teams.
summary:
Lunar Window is a landing-window planner for the lunar south pole.

Existing tools ask you to pick a site and a date, then show you the sky. Lunar Window starts from what a mission needs (sunlight at landing, how long it survives darkness, a direct line to Earth) and shows every site and every landing day that works across a year, on one screen. When the launch slips, you drag one control and see which sites survive, which fail, and why.

For any site and moment it shows the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain horizon, the solar elevation, the time until sunset and until the Earth sets, and a first-person 3D view built from NASA LOLA elevation data, with real shadows. Any point of the Moon can be entered and gets its real terrain. It opens with a two-minute guided landing, voiced as Mission Control, that can be skipped.

It matters because at the pole one ridge decides whether a lander has power and radio, and schedules move. Accuracy is measured and published in the tool: Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.004°, and the terrain horizon reproduces NASA's LOLA illumination maps to 1.6 percentage points on average.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A guided first landing. The tool opens with it: out of the dark, Mission Control calls on the radio and, in two minutes, talks you through one real case while you fly the tool yourself: a lander due at Malapert Massif on 17 January 2027, a launch that slips three weeks, the site that goes dark and the two that still work. Every step asks for one thing in the real interface, which is ringed while the rest of the screen dims. It can be skipped, done for you, or taken again from the Guide button, in English, Portuguese or Spanish.

Explore. Pick one of 15 curated sites (Artemis candidate regions, CLPS landing sites, Apollo, and landers from India, Japan and China) and any date from 1969 to 2035. The tool shows at once whether the Sun is up and whether the Earth is in view, the solar elevation, how much of the solar disc clears the terrain, and the time until the next sunset and the next loss of Earth contact. "Stand there" puts you on the site in 3D: real LOLA terrain with shadows cast by the low Sun, the Sun and the Earth at their true size and position, the Earth with its real phase and rotation, and the real stars when the Sun is hidden. A 360° horizon panorama and a 30-day timeline give the same answer as a chart. Going from one place to another, the Moon is shown whole (the map of the LRO camera, lit as it is at that moment) and the camera comes down to the ground of the new place without a cut.

Any point of the Moon. Type a latitude and longitude, or click the map of the south pole: the point gets its real terrain, computed in the browser from NASA's LOLA elevation models in a few seconds: its horizon, its 3D view, its row in the landing-window calendar. The model is 80 m per pixel from the south pole to 82°S and 474 m everywhere else. No site and no point uses a smooth Moon.

Check with NASA. The site file gives the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and the Earth to a thousandth of a degree, with a link that asks NASA's JPL Horizons System the same question for that place and moment.

A telescope on the planets. In the night sky of a site the five planets visible to the eye are named where they really are; click one and a telescope shows it at its true size, phase and tilt for that moment.

Plan a mission. State the requirements: days on the surface, Sun at landing, the longest darkness the lander survives, Earth in view at landing, the longest loss of contact, the height of the solar panel and antenna (0, 2 or 10 m), and the margin the antenna needs above the terrain. The calendar shows, for every site and every landing day of a year, whether the mission is viable. Drag the launch slip and the summary updates: "A 21-day slip moves the landing to 7 Feb 2027. 2 of 9 south-pole sites still work." Click any cell to see which requirement failed and by how much. A map of the south pole, built from the LOLA elevation model with the permanently shadowed ground in black, shows where the sites are and which of them still work on the landing day.

Landing error. Real landers miss their target. For every polar site the planner also tests eight points 250 m around it and reports at how many of the nine the plan still holds.

Compare. Up to four combinations of site and landing day side by side.

Missions. Three planning problems to play, scored only on real quantities: tolerance to landing error, room for a further delay, and time lost.

Replay. Seven real landings can be replayed at their real place and minute, with the sourced facts next to what the tool shows.

Accuracy. A page inside the tool gives the measured errors, the method and the limits.

HOW IT WORKS

Terrain. For each polar site an offline tool reads NASA LOLA elevation models (5 m per pixel near seven of the sites, 80 m and 240 m beyond) and computes the elevation of the horizon in 1440 directions, with the curvature of the Moon, for observers 0, 2 and 10 m above the ground. For a point of the visitor's own the same method runs in a web worker, on the same NASA models cut in pieces that the browser fetches on demand.

Sun and Earth. The JPL Horizons service cannot be called from a browser, so the positions are computed in the browser (astronomy-engine with the IAU rotation model of the Moon) and tested against Horizons tables. One computation per instant serves every site.

Planner. A year of positions for 15 sites and 72 surrounding points is computed in a web worker in about one second. There is no server: the tool is a static page and keeps working offline once loaded. A scenario is a link that can be sent to a colleague, and the calendar exports to CSV.

WHAT WAS MEASURED

- Sun and Earth against JPL Horizons, 2946 positions at nine places and periods from 1969 to 2031: largest error 0.0033° in elevation.

- Terrain horizon against NASA's LOLA average-illumination maps, 144 points over 33 x 33 km: mean absolute error 1.6 percentage points for the Sun and 1.0 for the Earth; correlation 0.93 and 0.99.

- At the scale of a single 60 m pixel on a ridge the agreement drops (correlation 0.66), which is why the planner reports the result for the area around the point.

- Terrain of any point: the pieces the browser uses differ from the full polar models by 0.002° on average. Away from the pole the global model (474 m per pixel) differs from the finer polar models by 0.19° at the median, and by several degrees on steep ground.

- Height matters: at Connecting Ridge the Sun is visible 51% of the time at ground level, 89% at 2 m and 93% at 10 m.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO

Only the two constraints named by the challenge are modelled: sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth. Temperature, slopes, hazards, relay satellites and trajectories are not. The mission profiles are examples, not the requirements of any real mission. Away from the south pole the terrain model is 474 m per pixel, coarser than at the pole, and the Accuracy page gives what that costs.

WHO IT IS FOR AND WHAT COMES NEXT

Mission planners who need a first answer in seconds when a schedule moves; educators and the public who want to see why the lunar south pole is hard. Next steps: relay-satellite coverage, thermal constraints, finer terrain away from the pole, and a view of the site for VR headsets.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Vite, three.js, astronomy-engine, Vitest; Python with NumPy for the offline terrain tools; FFmpeg; OpenAI text-to-speech for the voice of the guide and of the video (declared below); GitHub Pages.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA south polar elevation models LDEM_80S_80M, LDEM_75S_240M, LDEM_60S_240M (NASA PDS Geosciences Node)
LRO LOLA global elevation model LDEM_64 (NASA PDS Geosciences Node)
LOLA 5 m/pixel south pole site elevation models (NASA GSFC Planetary Geodesy Data Archive, product 78)
LOLA average illumination maps AVGVISIB_85S_060M, Sun and Earth (LOLA team, NASA GSFC)
LROC Anthropogenic Features on the Moon (coordinates of real landing sites)
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio: CGI Moon Kit (LRO camera colour map of the Moon)
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio: Deep Star Maps 2020 (Milky Way)
NASA GIBS: VIIRS Corrected Reflectance, Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 (the face of the Earth)
NASA 3D Resources: Space Exploration Vehicle, Apollo Lunar Module, maps of Jupiter, Saturn and Mars
projectRefs: Full list of every resource used, with licences (REFERENCES.md)
Source code of the project (MIT licence)
astronomy-engine (MIT): positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon in the browser
ESA Gaia DR2 (ESA/Gaia/DPAC), in the Milky Way map
Yale Bright Star Catalogue, JSON edition by Bretton Wade (MIT)
OpenAI text-to-speech: the AI-generated voice of the guide and of the demo video
Poly Haven (CC0): scanned rocks and surface textures
Vite, TypeScript, Vitest (MIT / Apache-2.0): build and tests
NumPy and Pillow: offline terrain and texture tools
glTF-Transform (MIT): re-encoding the NASA models for the web
FFmpeg: encoding of the guide voice and of the demo video
Gläser et al. 2018, Illumination conditions at the lunar poles (reading)
Wueller et al. 2026, candidate landing sites in the Artemis exploration regions (data)
